q: Two electric charges, which are not in contact, exert electrical forces on each other.
e: True. Two electric charges, which are not in contact, exert electrical forces on each other. Charges act at a distance. We describe that action with an electric field.

q: The concept of gravitational field is used to explain the phenomenon of electrical forces between charges not in contact.
e: False. Electrical forces are explained with an electric field, not a gravitational field.

q: Just as there is a gravitational force between two masses, there is an electric force between two charges.
e: True. Just as there is a gravitational force between two masses, there is an electric force between two charges. Coulomb's law is K Q1 Q2 / r² along the line joining the charges.

q: Electrical forces bind electrons and nuclei to form molecules.
e: False. Electrical forces bind electrons and nuclei to form atoms. Molecules come from atoms bonding.

q: Gravitational forces are appreciable only when the masses of the bodies are very large.
e: True. Gravitational forces are appreciable only when the masses of the bodies are very large. Gravity only shows clearly when the masses are huge.

q: Electrical forces are so much smaller in magnitude than gravitational forces.
e: False. Electrical forces are far stronger than gravitational forces, not smaller.

q: Coulomb's law states that the electric force between two charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
e: True. Coulomb's law states that the electric force between two charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Coulomb's law: F = K q1 q2 / r². Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

q: In the SI system, charge $Q$ is measured in coulomb, the distance $r$ in metre and the force $F$ in joule.
e: False. Coulomb's law: F = K q1 q2 / r². Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

q: $\epsilon$ is a constant called the permittivity of the medium in which the charges are located.
e: True. Ε is a constant called the permittivity of the medium in which the charges are located. K depends on the units and on the permittivity of the medium. In vacuum K = 1/(4πε0) = 9 × 10⁹.

q: When charges are located in vacuum, $K = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon}$.
e: False. Coulomb's law is K Q1 Q2 / r² along the line joining the charges. The written line says When charges are located in vacuum, K = (1)/(4πε).

q: $\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of vacuum, $\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}$.
e: True. Ε_0 is the permittivity of vacuum, ε_0 = 8.85 × 10^-12 C²N^-1m^-2. ε0 is 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻².

q: For convenience in calculation, the value of $K$ in vacuum will be taken as $K = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ Nm}^2\text{C}^{-2}$.
e: True. For convenience in calculation, the value of K in vacuum will be taken as K = 9 × 10^9 Nm²C^-2. In vacuum take K as 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².

q: The value of $K$ in air is approximately equal to that of $K$ in water.
e: False. The written claim is the opposite of the chapter fact. The written line says The value of K in air is approximately equal to that of K in water.

q: Electric force is a vector quantity.
e: True. Electric force is a vector quantity. Electric has to stay in that role in the sentence.

q: The direction of electric force is always perpendicular to the line joining the two charges.
e: False. Coulomb's law is K Q1 Q2 / r² along the line joining the charges. The written line says The direction of electric force is always perpendicular to the line joining the two charges.

q: If the charges are like charges, the force between them is repulsive and is directed outwards.
e: True. If the charges are like charges, the force between them is repulsive and is directed outwards. Like charges push apart. The force arrows point outward along the line joining them.

q: If the charges are unlike charges, the electric force between them is attractive and is directed inwards.
e: True. If the charges are unlike charges, the electric force between them is attractive and is directed inwards. Like charges push apart. The force arrows point outward along the line joining them.

q: Since the electric force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the two charges, Coulomb's law is also called an inverse square law.
e: True. Since the electric force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the two charges, Coulomb's law is also called an inverse square law. Coulomb's law: F = K q1 q2 / r². Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

q: A point charge is a charge without dimension or with dimension so much smaller than other dimensions appearing in the problem.
e: True. A point charge is a charge without dimension or with dimension so much smaller than other dimensions appearing in the problem. A point charge is small enough that its own size can be ignored next to the other distances.
